quote: In our ancestral environment, there were no movies; what you saw with your own eyes was true.
content: The contrast is between seeing what happened and seeing what never happened, and perception, for all its errors, is anchored to the first. Eyewitness failures concern memory for strangers' faces under stress and suggestion, which is why they fill wrongful-conviction files (Loftus 1975). They are not evidence that our ancestors routinely saw events that did not occur. The essay then dissolves the distinction between seeing and reading on purpose; that is its argument, not a lapse. The evolved heuristic treats vivid sight as true and dry text as story. The essay concludes that both are causal chains from the event and deserve weight according to their reliability, not their vividness.

quote: I should try to think as if everything I read about in history books had actually happened to me.
content: Imagination inflation makes people believe an event happened to them. The essay's proposal is ironic about exactly that, "I remember; I wasn't there," and asks for the weight of history, not a false memory. It also builds in the correction the note says is missing: "With appropriate reweighting for the availability bias of history books—I should remember being a thousand peasants for every ruler." Khong's decision-makers went wrong by leaning on one vivid analogy. Neustadt and May's cure in Thinking in Time is broader and deeper historical knowledge, so that no single case dominates (1986, book, no DOI). The essay prescribes remembering every era, which is the opposite of remembering only Munich.

quote: So many mistakes, made over and over and over again, because I did not remember making them, in every era I never lived
content: Ambiguity afflicts the causes of particular events, but the lessons the essay draws are base rates. Mysterious answers to mysterious questions have failed every time they were tested; no generation predicted the world of the next; modern worlds have fallen before. None of those depends on which of Demandt's two hundred and ten causes brought down Rome. The essay's closing instruction, "Remember how, century after century, the world changed in ways you did not guess," is the least ambiguous lesson in the historical record and the one most often forgotten.
